title: Distributed prefetch coordinator and deceleration protocol to smooth GPU admission
creator: Sofia Martinez
description: Follow-up from the GPU capacity exhaustion incident on 2026-03-08. We observed sustained queue growth caused by uncoordinated prefetch and aggressive admission during autoscaler transitions. This ticket scopes a small-footprint distributed service (prefetch coordinator) plus a runtime-side 'deceleration protocol' that temporarily reduces aggressive prefetch/admission and ramps requests back up using a heuristics-driven window. Goal: reduce queue amplification during pool priming and prevent repeated fast-fail/eviction cycles while preserving tail latency for high-priority tenants.
reproduction_steps: 1) Start a dedicated GPU pool and enable aggressive prefetch (prefetch_factor >= 2.0) on several high-throughput tenants
2) Simulate a traffic spike by replaying a 2x burst of real traffic for 10 minutes with a mix of long-sequence generation requests
3) Trigger an autoscaler event (scale down followed by scale up) while prefetch tasks are in flight
4) Observe queue growth on the target pool, increased token wait times, and subsequent tenant-level evictions/fast-fails
timeline: 2026-03-08 02:14 UTC - Hosted API showed rising queue length on us-west-2-gpu-pool-7
2026-03-08 02:22 UTC - Autoscaler primed and provisioned additional nodes; prefetch tasks from existing workers continued to backfill
2026-03-08 02:40 UTC - Tenant requests started experiencing 503s and increased latency leading to customer support alerts
2026-03-09 09:00 UTC - Postmortem concluded uncoordinated prefetch combined with hysteresis in autoscaler caused queue amplification
2026-03-10 11:00 UTC - This ticket created to prototype coordinator + deceleration protocol
impact: High. Multiple hosted API tenants experienced increased tail latency and intermittent 5xx/503s for a rolling 45-minute window. Estimated request loss ~0.6% of peak traffic during incident. Several enterprise tenants engaged support with SLA concerns.
root_cause: Concurrency between local worker prefetch logic and autoscaler-driven topology changes caused many in-flight prefetches to land on drained/evicted slots. Lack of a global admission smoothing primitive meant independent workers reissued prefetch/admission, amplifying queue length during capacity transitions.
decisions: Implement a lightweight distributed prefetch coordinator that maintains transient admission credits per pool and exposes a simple lease API for workers

Introduce a runtime-side deceleration protocol: after autoscaler events or observed queue spikes, workers enter a 'soft-deceleration' window where prefetch_factor is halved and new admissions are jittered
Priority tenants bypass full deceleration via tokenized fast-path but still respect reduced prefetch credits
Keep coordinator state ephemeral (no durable DB) and use gRPC with exponential backoff; design for lossy networking and eventual consistency
Roll out in canary: start with non-critical pools, then broaden if metrics show reduced amplification without latency regressions

metrics_to_track: pool.queue_length.p95 - target: decrease by >= 30% in canary pools
pool.prefetch_inflight.count - target: decrease by >= 40% during decel windows
tenant.5xx_rate - target: return to baseline within 10 minutes of autoscaler events
avg_token_wait_ms - watch for regressions vs baseline (acceptable <10% increase for priority tenants)
coord.leases_granted_per_min - sanity check for coordinator availability
notes: Tradeoffs: ephemeral coordinator avoids ops burden but increases risk of transient lease loss; mitigated by permissive fallback behavior in workers
We intentionally avoid centralized throttling per-tenant to keep tenant isolation guarantees intact; coordinator operates at pool-level credits
Longer-term: evaluate adding prewarm handoff signal from autoscaler to coordinator so prefetch can be drained gracefully before scale events
Customer comms: target proactive outreach to enterprise tenants affected; draft available in links
